4.0.s.en: (1) The enemies' mockery and threat of war

4.0.0.en: Sanballat was governor of Samaria on behalf of the Persian kingdom. When he heard the news that the Jews were determined to build a wall around their city Jerusalem, he was greatly angered and enraged at this for the following reasons:

4.0.1.en: 1- The Samaritans believed only in the five books of Moses and offered their worship with images at Bethel and Dan in their land, whereas the Jews believed in all the books of the prophets and offered their worship in the temple at Jerusalem. The building of the wall encourages worship in the temple, and so the deficiency of the Samaritans appears by comparison with those living in Jerusalem and Judea.

4.0.2.en: 2- The Samaritans intermarried with pagan foreigners, which is against the Law of Moses, and this was rejected by the Jews in Jerusalem. Therefore the building of the wall shows the strength of the Jews and their condemnation of what the Samaritans were doing. Sanballat and all those with him were enraged; they were Samaritans, who were originally Jews, but their mingling with the pagans in their worship made him mock the Jews' building of the wall of their city. This shows the extent of his pride, but at the same time it shows his weakness, because he was enraged: he is proud, but inwardly feels weakness before the power of Jerusalem and its temple.

4.0.3.en: Sanballat's pride made him despise the Jews and not try to stop them by force from building the wall, content to mock them. This was by God's permission, so that Nehemiah might begin building the wall and the Jews be encouraged and not neglect the oppositions of the enemies that would come upon them one after another.

4.0.4.en: Do not attack others with mockery, thinking it is humor, for this shows how evil your heart is, and your pride and lack of love for others, and even your contempt for them. There is a great difference between gentle humor that makes people happy and condemning others and mocking them, even if they do not answer you out of their politeness and shyness.

4.1.0.en: His brethren: his senior assistants from the Samaritans in leadership, that is, the chiefs of the people. When Sanballat was enraged, he gathered the chiefs of the people and the commanders of the armies of the Samaritans and began to show his contempt and mockery of the Jews and his confidence in the impossibility of the Jews' being able to build the wall, which appeared in the following:

4.1.1.en: 1- "What do these feeble Jews?" The Assyrian kingdom and then after it the Babylonian kingdom took the best of the Jews to help in the capital of the kingdom and left in Jerusalem and Judea the weak and poor of the people. Therefore Sanballat despised them, declaring with confidence their inability to do a huge work, namely building a wall for Jerusalem, not knowing that the power of God is able to work through the weak.

4.1.2.en: 2- "Will they fortify themselves?" The second reason for the impossibility of building the wall is that the Persian kingdom would not allow the Jews to build this wall, so that all the cities would remain weak and under the control of the Persians.

4.1.3.en: 3- "Will they sacrifice?" With contempt he asserted that they would not be able to complete the wall and then rejoice in it and offer sacrifices to God in thanksgiving and joy at the completion of the work.

4.1.4.en: 4- "Will they make an end in a day?" In view of the hugeness of the wall and its great area, Sanballat showed that it needed a long time, which he imagined would be years, so he said that the zeal of the Jews seemed as if they would complete the wall in a day, and this was impossible in his view.

4.1.5.en: 5- "Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?" The last obstacle is that the Babylonians burned the old wall, so the stones lying around the broken wall are burned and covered with heaps of rubbish, and it is hard to bring them out and renew them to rebuild the wall.

4.2.0.en: Present at this meeting with Sanballat was Tobiah the Ammonite, who was chief of the children of Ammon, enemies of the Jews who lived beside the Jews to the east of their land. He joined Sanballat in mocking the Jews and added a sixth point confirming the inability of the Jews to build a strong wall for their city. He said that even if the Jews built a wall it would be so weak that a small, light animal like a fox, if it walked on it, would bring it down, and the fox would not need to use its cunning to bring the wall down, because the wall would be so weak that it would fall of itself if the fox walked on it.

4.3.0.en: Nehemiah did not answer the enemies' mockery but lifted his heart to God in prayer, because it is God who fights for His children and He is their refuge in all their needs. His prayer included the following matters:

4.3.2.en: He asked God to listen attentively to his prayer, and the people may have joined him in repeating this prayer. And in order to win God's heart he said to Him, we are Your people and Your children, whom the Gentiles mock and reproach, and this of course does not please You because You love Your children.

4.3.3.en: 2- "Turn their reproach upon their own head"

4.3.4.en: He asked God to turn the mockery of the enemies back upon their own heads if they persisted in their evil, for divine justice demands the punishment of the wicked. This is not a feeling of vengeance or hatred on Nehemiah's part but a showing forth of divine justice, in the hope that through the discipline of the wicked and the success of the righteous all may be led to faith.

4.3.5.en: 3- "Give them for a prey in the land of captivity"

4.3.6.en: As a discipline from God, Nehemiah asks for the defeat of these enemies in wars, so that they are exposed to the plundering and seizure of their spoils, in the hope that all this may lead them to faith and repentance.

4.3.7.en: 4- "Cover not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before thee"

4.3.8.en: He asks God to continue His discipline of the wicked and not forgive them by blotting out their sins or covering them, but to keep punishing them until they repent; and if they persist in evil, their punishment will be a lesson to others, that they may repent.

4.3.9.en: 5- "For they have provoked thee to anger before the builders"

4.3.10.en: The sin of the enemies is magnified in that they angered the God of the children of Israel before the Jews who were building the wall, with the intention of bringing a spirit of doubt and despair into them, so that they would stop the work and God would consequently be angry with them.

4.4.0.en: "All the wall was joined together unto the half thereof": that is, they built the wall around the whole city in a complete circuit but at half the height; so it became a complete wall but still low. Nehemiah and the Jews did not heed the enemies' reproaches but continued to work for God's sake, who is more important than any person, and pleasing Him is above all. Indeed, these reproaches spurred the Jews to zeal in the work so as to show the power of God that supported them and complete the wall in the shortest time, and they built with a heart turned toward God and in unity to accomplish the work.

4.4.1.en: When Satan fights you, do not be disturbed but resist him, firmly rooted in faith, drive away his thoughts and refuse his lusts, confident that you have authority over him. Continue building your spiritual life and pay no attention to thoughts of doubt and despair, for all of them are from Satan and are not from logic or reality, as he tries to deceive you. For however great your weakness, you are mighty through God who dwells in you.

4.5.s.en: (2) An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews

4.5.0.en: The Ashdodites: the inhabitants of Ashdod, one of the five great cities of the Philistines, in which was the temple of the god Dagon, who fell before the ark of the covenant of God in the days of Samuel the prophet (1 Sam 5:3). They were greatly afraid then, but with time they forgot the fear of the God of Israel and allied themselves to fight the Jews. The breaches: the plural of breach, which is a gap inside the wall.

4.5.1.en: The lands surrounding Jerusalem, when they heard of the building of its wall, were angry, because they feared that Jerusalem would become a power and fight them. So they allied together to fight it, to stop the building of its walls and to kill the workers building the wall. These lands did not have strong relations between one another, but they allied themselves in evil to oppose the city of God.

4.6.0.en: Nehemiah was not disturbed but encouraged the rulers and the people, and they prayed to God, and with the help of the rulers he set guards ready for war and for the defense of Jerusalem.

4.6.1.en: We notice here two things that Nehemiah did: the first is prayer and after it the guarding of Jerusalem. He began with prayer because God is the Giver of strength, and then he did his duty, which was guarding the city.

4.6.2.en: In all your problems and projects, indeed in all your works, begin with prayer, and at the same time do not be lax in carrying out your duty with all exactness. However great your weakness, God will complete you and make you succeed.

4.7.0.en: A new opposition began after the three previous oppositions, which are:

4.7.1.en: 1- Accusing the Jews of rebelling against the state (2:19).

4.7.3.en: 3- Plotting a war to stop the building of the wall and to harm Jerusalem (ch. 4:8).

4.7.4.en: 4- And this opposition is the one found in this verse, and it came from the Jews themselves, from the tribe of Judah, that is, those living in Jerusalem and Judea, for they declared that the work was huge and that the rubbish they carried, which lay around the wall, was very great, and the carriers no longer had strength to continue the work of removing this rubbish. These voices were from Jews who were informants for the enemies, spreading a spirit of doubt and weakness among those working in the building, as they declared their inability to continue the work and spread this among the people. Thus two oppositions joined together, namely the war plotted by the enemies with the spirit of doubt and the weakening of the resolve of those working on the wall.

4.7.5.en: Do not be disturbed if the wicked gather against you and afflictions multiply, for they are worthless before the power of God that is in you. Seek God and persevere in your striving, and be faithful in your work, confident in the power of God, which overcomes those who oppose you.

4.8.0.en: The enemies plotted a military plan for a sudden attack on Jerusalem, so that the enemies would infiltrate and the Jews would be surprised by the war launched against them with the enemies in their midst fighting them.

4.8.1.en: But God's grace supported Nehemiah, and the secret news of the war plotted against them reached him. Most likely it came from Jews living beside the enemies, who were faithful to their city and did not fear the enemies, and they informed Nehemiah of what was being plotted against Jerusalem.

4.9.0.en: From all places whence ye shall return unto us: all the lands outside Jerusalem in which Jews dwell beside the enemies, and from which they returned to their holy city Jerusalem, whether to take part in building the wall or only to report this military plot.

4.9.1.en: Many of the Jews living outside Jerusalem and those working on the building of the wall confirmed the news of this plotted war, and they informed Nehemiah ten times, that is, many times, of this plotted war.

4.10.0.en: Their bows: the plural of bow, which is used for shooting arrows.

4.10.1.en: Nehemiah organized the guarding of the wall and the city. He stationed guards behind the parts of the wall whose building was not complete, that is, where the wall was still low, and then in the places where the wall had risen and was complete he stationed guards, referred to as the higher places of the wall. Thus he arranged a guard around the whole city and was not disturbed that the wall was incomplete.

4.10.2.en: The organization of the guard was with wisdom on Nehemiah's part, for the guards stood according to their clans, each clan guarding a certain part, so that cooperation among them would be easy because of their kinship to one another.

4.10.3.en: Most likely he stationed archers with bows on the high places, and in the low places, that is, on the ground behind the low wall, the men carried swords and spears. He was confident in the power of God that was with them. For though the enemies were trained men of war and the Jews were weak and untrained in war, Nehemiah made every possible preparation and relied on God, the Guardian of his city.

4.11.0.en: Nehemiah took care to encourage the rulers and the people who were ready for war, declaring the invincible supporting power of God. For Nehemiah is a popular leader who takes care to persuade everyone to defend their city bravely and in faith, and he is a thoughtful leader who looks at and investigates the matter and then rises to plan and distribute the work and encourage the workers to guard the city. Nehemiah took care to stir up the zeal and jealousy of the people to defend their city, because in it were their wives, their children and their homes, since they would not accept being taken captive or killed by the enemies.

4.12.s.en: (3) Nehemiah's preparation for war while completing the building

4.12.0.en: Sanballat and Tobiah and all their followers among the enemies learned that their plots for a sudden invasion of Jerusalem had been discovered by the people of God, who had prepared for them and did not fear their power. So their plots failed and the people of God returned, each one to his work on the wall; that is, they were not held back by these threats, but the people of God felt His power supporting them and bringing the plots of the enemies to nothing, so they rejoiced and were firm in their faith.

4.13.0.en: Spears: the plural of spear, which is a metal rod pointed at its end, a weapon of war for stabbing the enemy.

4.13.1.en: Shields: the plural of shield, which is a piece of wood covered with leather with a handle at the back, into which the soldier puts his hand and moves the shield in front of his face and body to protect him from arrows.

4.13.2.en: Habergeons: the plural of habergeon, which is metal clothing covering the chest and stomach to protect the soldier from arrows and spears or any weapon of war.

4.13.3.en: With wisdom Nehemiah divided those working with him into two parts: the first part built the wall, and the second part bore arms to guard the wall from the attacks of the enemies.

4.13.4.en: And they carried the various weapons used in war at that time:

4.13.5.en: The rulers did their work of encouraging those who built the wall or those who guarded it, so that they would accomplish their works for God's sake. A part of the workers devoted themselves to bearing arms, which had two benefits: the guarding of the wall, and also a rest for the guards from the toil of building, so that they might regain their strength and then return to the hard work of building, which some had begun to tire of because of the great amount of rubbish they were carrying (v. 10).

4.14.0.en: The meaning of this is that half of the men worked on building the wall, whether in laying stones or carrying earth, and the other half guarded the wall. To express this it says that with one hand they built and with the other they held a weapon, that is, half of them built and the other half guarded. It does not of course mean that he carried a load with one hand and held a weapon in the other hand, for that is not practical.

4.15.0.en: Besides dividing the workers into a part for guarding and a part for building, the workers also each carried his sword on his thigh, and most likely it was a small sword that did not hinder the worker's movement in building, whereas the one responsible for guarding carried the various weapons mentioned before in v. 16. Nehemiah himself inspected the work on the wall and encouraged the builders and the guards, and beside him was a man carrying a large trumpet which, when he blew it, everyone in Jerusalem would hear its sound, in order to direct them and gather them when needed for war.

4.15.1.en: It is good in your spiritual striving to take care to guard your senses and thoughts and keep them away from every sin, and at the same time to take care of positive work such as prayers, readings and services, for the two complete each other for your spiritual growth.

4.16.0.en: Nehemiah agreed with the rulers who helped him in managing the city and with all the chiefs that they should teach the people working on building the wall, and the guards, that because of the wide extent of the wall it was hard for them to hear one another; therefore when they heard the trumpet they should gather to it, because Nehemiah and the trumpeter would remain at the place from which the enemies attacked, and by the blowing of the trumpet they would gather the people to the same place to repel the enemies' attack.

4.16.1.en: And this confirms many things, which are:

4.16.2.en: 1- That Nehemiah was inspecting and watching the work and the areas surrounding Jerusalem, that is, following the building and the preparation for the enemies' attacks.

4.16.3.en: 2- Although they bore arms everywhere on the wall to guard it, at the attack they gather with one heart, and God looks upon their love and their attachment to Him and to one another, and so He intervenes and fights the enemies for them. They gather to declare their unity, their submission to God and their faith in His power defending them.

4.16.4.en: 3- The trumpet signifies the word of God, which gathers the faithful into one mind, the mind of Christ, and He fights for them against the attacks of Satan.

4.17.0.en: The earnestness in the work is noticed here, from the break of dawn until full darkness when the stars appear, and therefore the guard too was complete from dawn to night.

4.17.1.en: Seize the opportunity of life to work faithfully. This life is signified by the day, as Christ says, "Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you" (Jn 12:35). So as long as you are able to worship God and serve Him, and to be faithful in every work for His sake, you must work before the darkness comes, that is, death.

4.18.0.en: Nehemiah also took care to guard Jerusalem and its wall all night long, so he made some of the men lodge with their helpers in the midst of Jerusalem and inside its walls; that is, not all lodged in their homes, but he organized a night guard as he organized the day guard.

4.19.0.en: Nehemiah and his relatives, helpers and guards were an example to the rest of the men in activity all day long, for they did not take off their clothes and their weapons, in order to continue the work however long the day. The only exception to taking off the clothes was when they went to the water to wash and bathe.

4.19.2.en: 1- If the previous chapter tells us about the external enemies who stood against the people of God to prevent them from building the wall, this chapter tells us about the internal troubles among the people of God, such as injustice and the exploitation of the weak.

4.19.3.en: 2- The events of this chapter did not happen during the building of the wall, but began a long time earlier, either in the days of Nehemiah or before his governorship over Jerusalem. Then the poor presented their complaints near the end of the period of Nehemiah's governorship, which lasted twelve years, as is shown by what is mentioned in (v. 14). This is because the troubles of the poor had increased, and on the other hand they found in Nehemiah the good and just governor who could do them justice and have compassion on them.
